paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion samplers can reduce computation by generating selected spectral coordinates and filling the remaining directions with noise. How many directions must they retain? We study this question for data with power-law covariance spectra. For Gaussian data compared to a smoothed target, we prove matching bounds on the required number of retained directions, provided that the ambient dimension is sufficiently large. The truncation error depends on the combined Wiener gains of the omitted directions, regardless of the accuracy of the sampler on the retained coordinates. Keeping only directions whose signal exceeds the output noise level can therefore leave a non-vanishing error: many individually weak directions remain significant in aggregate. Combining this characterization with a diffusion convergence bound yields sufficient sampling-step complexity under exact scores. The upper bounds also extend to estimated principal components and, componentwise, to Gaussian mixtures. The practical prescription is to select the retained subspace using an aggregate spectral-tail error budget, then to choose the diffusion noise level accordingly.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models generate data by learning to reverse a process that gradually adds noise ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2020 ) . Their computational cost typically grows with the dimension of the space in which the diffusion runs, motivating approaches that exploit alternative representations of the data. Examples include diffusion in wavelet coordinates ( Guth et al., 2022 ) , frequency-dependent processes such as blurring diffusion and inverse-heat-dissipation models ( Hoogeboom and Salimans, 2023 ; Rissanen et al., 2023 ) , and diffusion restricted to lower-dimensional subspaces ( Jing et al., 2022 ) . Related approaches operate in learned autoencoder representations, including VAE-based latent spaces ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , which need not correspond to orthogonal transformations. Here, we focus on orthogonal representations, such as principal-component, Fourier, and wavelet bases, in which the distribution of signal across directions can be described explicitly. An orthogonal change of basis preserves the ambient dimension, but it can reveal a structure that a sampler can exploit. For images, a central example is spectral decay: natural-image spectra are often approximately described by power laws ( Field, 1987 ; Ruderman, 1994 ; Hyvärinen et al., 2009 ) . In a corresponding coefficient model, the variances satisfy σ i 2 ≍ i − β \sigma_{i}^{2}\asymp i^{-\beta} , so a small number of directions carry much of the variance, while many others contain progressively weaker signals. This unequal distribution of signals suggests that the effort needed to generate different coordinates should depend on their statistical importance. These observations motivate the question studied in this paper: how does spectral structure affect the convergence of diffusion samplers in an orthogonal representation and when can it reduce the sampling complexity? More specifically, under power-law spectral decay, how many directions must a sampler retain to achieve a prescribed accuracy at a given resolution, and how many sampling steps are sufficient on those directions? Answering these questions requires controlling both the convergence of the sampler on the retained coordinates and the approximation error from replacing the remaining coordinates with noise. Our analysis connects these two costs, quantifying when sampling complexity can be governed by the number of required directions rather than by the ambient dimension.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: • The exact cost of truncation. For Gaussian data, replacing the discarded directions by noise costs, in total variation, a quantity of the order of the Euclidean norm of their Wiener gains g i = σ i 2 / ( σ i 2 + η 2 ) g_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{2}/(\sigma_{i}^{2}+\eta^{2}) , with matching upper and lower bounds (Theorem 1 ). The lower bound holds for every sampler of this kind, however accurate it is on the retained directions. • How many directions must be kept. Under a power law, accuracy ε \varepsilon at resolution η \eta requires, and is achieved with K ≍ β ( C / ( η 2 ε ) ) 2 / ( 2 ​ β − 1 ) K\asymp_{\beta}\bigl(C/(\eta^{2}\varepsilon)\bigr)^{2/(2\beta-1)} retained directions (Theorem 2 ), strictly more than the number of directions above the noise level. • End-to-end sampling complexity. For the reverse diffusion on the retained coordinates, with direction-dependent rates, the number of steps depends on the number of retained directions and not on the ambient dimension (Theorem 3 ). Choosing the diffusion noise level from K K gives O ~ ( ε − 4 β / ( 2 β − 1 ) ) \widetilde{O}\bigl(\varepsilon^{-4\beta/(2\beta-1)}\bigr) reverse steps with an exact score. The upper bounds extend to the principal components estimated from the data and to patch-based Gaussian mixtures (Section 5 ).

sections.heading: Related work.
sections.text: Our lower bound is based on the two-sided total-variation bound for Gaussians of Devroye et al. (2018) ; what we add is the identification of the relevant covariance ratios with the Wiener gains of the discarded directions, and a projection argument that makes the bound hold for every truncated sampler. The convergence analysis extends the Girsanov argument of Chen et al. (2022) to anisotropic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. In the retained subspace, isotropic diffusion attains the same step count up to constants (Proposition 3 ), so the gain comes from choosing which directions to keep, not from how they are diffused. Preconditioned samplers ( Ma et al., 2022 ) use anisotropy to speed up sampling rather than to decide what to discard. A longer discussion is in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Organisation.
sections.text: Section 2 introduces the data model and the truncated sampler. Section 3 proves the sharp bounds on truncation, and Section 4 the convergence of the sampler and its end-to-end complexity. Section 5 treats empirical bases and Gaussian mixtures. Section 6 reports experiments, and Section 7 discusses implications.

sections.heading: 2 Problem Setup and Truncated Sampler
sections.text: We first fix the data model, then the diffusion that generates the retained coordinates, and finally the class of truncated samplers and the target against which they are judged.

sections.heading: 2.1 Data model

We use a power-law envelope to allow unequal variances without imposing a low-dimensional support; Gaussianity is an additional condition for the sharp truncation results. sections.heading: 2.3 Truncated samplers and their target
sections.text: A truncated sampler generates the retained coefficients and fills every other direction with noise. To compare it with the full-dimensional data, we add Gaussian noise of a fixed level η > 0 \eta>0 to all outputs: given U ^ ∼ p \widehat{U}\sim p , it returns X ~ η = V K ​ ( U ^ + ξ ) + V ⟂ ​ Z , \widetilde{X}^{\eta}=V_{K}\bigl(\widehat{U}+\xi\bigr)+V_{\perp}Z, where ξ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , η 2 ​ I K ) \xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\eta^{2}I_{K}) , Z ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , η 2 ​ I d − K ) Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\eta^{2}I_{d-K}) , V ⟂ = [ v K + 1 , … , v d ] V_{\perp}=[v_{K+1},\ldots,v_{d}] , and U ^ , ξ , Z \widehat{U},\xi,Z are independent. Definition 1 (Truncated samplers) . For K ≤ d K\leq d , η > 0 \eta>0 and a probability law p p on ℝ K \mathbb{R}^{K} , the truncated sampler is the law p ~ η = ( p ∗ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , η 2 ​ I K ) ) ⊗ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , η 2 ​ I d − K ) , \widetilde{p}^{\eta}=\bigl(p*\mathcal{N}(0,\eta^{2}I_{K})\bigr)\otimes\mathcal{N}(0,\eta^{2}I_{d-K}), (8) written in the coordinates of the basis V V . The level η \eta acts as a resolution: a sampler is judged on the structure that remains visible after noise of level η \eta is added, and is not required to reproduce finer detail. Some such smoothing is unavoidable, because without it a truncated sampler produces laws supported on a K K -dimensional subspace, whose total-variation distance to a full-rank data law equals one however accurate the sampler is. The same smoothed target arises for early-stopped diffusion samplers, which return, up to a rescaling, the data law corrupted by a small amount of Gaussian noise ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Benton et al., 2023 ) ; Appendix B.6 makes this precise. For non-Gaussian data the truncation error additionally contains the dependence between retained and discarded coordinates (Section 5 ).

sections.heading: Two noise levels.
sections.text: The diffusion noise level σ \sigma belongs to the sampler: it sets the stationary law, the rates ( 5 ) and the count d eff σ d_{\mathrm{eff}}^{\sigma} . The evaluation level η \eta belongs to the target. The two are chosen separately: Section 3 shows that η \eta and the accuracy determine how many directions must be retained, and Section 4 then chooses σ \sigma small enough that all of them lie above the diffusion noise level. Together, the two sections answer the question of this paper: given a resolution η \eta and an accuracy ε \varepsilon , how many directions K K must a truncated sampler retain, and how many reverse steps N N does the sampler ( 7 ) need, to achieve TV ⁡ ( p ~ η , q η ) ≤ ε \mathrm{TV}(\widetilde{p}^{\eta},q^{\eta})\leq\varepsilon ?

First, the cost of discarding a direction is a denoising quantity: it depends on the direction only through its Wiener gain at the evaluation level. A direction whose signal dominates the noise ( g i g_{i} close to one) cannot be dropped without a constant error. It concerns the construction of Section 2.3 , in which the discarded directions are filled with Gaussian noise, and is not a lower bound for models that represent those directions in some other way.

sections.heading: 4 Diffusion Convergence and Sampling Complexity
sections.text: This section bounds the sampling error TV ⁡ ( p , q K ) \mathrm{TV}(p,q_{K}) in ( 10 ) for the reverse sampler ( 7 ), and then combines it with Section 3 into an end-to-end guarantee.

sections.heading: 4.1 Assumptions
sections.text: The assumptions separate properties of the target distribution from the accuracy and growth of the score used by the sampler. They concern only the coefficients retained in ℝ K \mathbb{R}^{K} and follow the Girsanov framework of Chen et al. (2022) . We state them for sampling down to time 0 0 . For data without a smooth density, Appendix D instead targets a positive-time marginal: regularity is then required of that smoothed law, rather than of the raw data. Positive-time smoothing alone does not assert the uniform Lipschitz bound below for every data law. Assumption 2 (Score regularity) . sections.heading: Why these conditions are reasonable.
sections.text: The Gaussian model provides an explicit example satisfying all four conditions. Its forward variance in coordinate i i is v i ​ ( t ) = e − 2 ​ λ i ​ t ​ σ i 2 + ( 1 − e − 2 ​ λ i ​ t ) ​ σ 2 , v_{i}(t)=e^{-2\lambda_{i}t}\sigma_{i}^{2}+(1-e^{-2\lambda_{i}t})\sigma^{2}, so the score is − u i / v i ( t ) -u_{i}/v_{i}(t) and is uniformly Lipschitz with L ≤ max ⁡ { σ K − 2 , σ − 2 } L\leq\max\{\sigma_{K}^{-2},\sigma^{-2}\} . For the exact power law and K ≤ d eff σ K\leq d_{\mathrm{eff}}^{\sigma} , this gives L ≤ σ − 2 L\leq\sigma^{-2} . Gaussian tails justify the integrations by parts; positive variances give a finite initial KL; and the exact score is linear, hence admissible, with zero score error. Thus, the end-to-end Gaussian result verifies these conditions directly rather than imposing an additional regularity model. For learned scores, Assumption 3 specifies the accuracy needed by the sampler. Its weighted mean-square norm is exactly the norm in the Girsanov drift mismatch, so errors in slower directions receive less weight. It is an accuracy requirement on the score, not a statement about how many training samples are needed to achieve it. A linear-growth constraint or clipping supplies admissibility; the accuracy condition must hold for the score actually used after any such modification. Finally, the spectral assumption already supplies the moment bound 𝔼 ​ ‖ U ‖ 2 = ∑ i ≤ K σ i 2 ≤ C sp ​ ζ ​ ( β ) \mathbb{E}\|U\|^{2}=\sum_{i\leq K}\sigma_{i}^{2}\leq C_{\mathrm{sp}}\zeta(\beta) , where ζ ⁡ ( β ) = ∑ i ≥ 1 i − β \zeta(\beta)=\sum_{i\geq 1}i^{-\beta} .

sections.text: The sharp truncation and end-to-end results use Gaussian data and a known principal-component basis; the retained-coordinate convergence theorem also applies to non-Gaussian laws. We now explain how the error decomposition accommodates general data, estimated bases and Gaussian mixtures. Precise statements and proofs are in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 6 Experimental Results
sections.text: We test the three modeling ingredients of the paper, a power-law spectrum, the Gaussian truncation bounds and Gaussian mixtures, in three settings (Appendix I ). (i) Covariance spectra of natural-image patches from CIFAR-10/100 ( Krizhevsky et al., 2009 ) , DIV2K ( Agustsson and Timofte, 2017 ) and BSDS500 ( Martin et al., 2001 ) , with patch sizes from 8 × 8 8\times 8 to 32 × 32 32\times 32 , to check Assumption 1 out of sample; audio frames from FMA ( Defferrard et al., 2017 ) are included for comparison(Appendix I ). (ii) Synthetic Gaussian data with an exact power law, on which every result of Sections 3-4 is checked (Appendix I.3.3 ). (iii) 8 × 8 × 3 8\times 8\times 3 patches of CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 modeled by Gaussian mixtures with up to 32 32 components ( Zoran and Weiss, 2012 ) . In (ii) and (iii) all densities are in closed form, so truncation errors are estimated by Monte Carlo without a learned discriminator. The code is available here .

sections.heading: 7 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: Truncating a diffusion model to a few spectral directions is attractive because natural data concentrate their variance, but it has a cost that no amount of training can remove: every truncated sampler pays at least the error of its discarded directions (Theorem 1 ). We quantify that cost and hence where to cut. Under a power-law spectrum the directions just below the noise level are as numerous as those above it, so their errors add up, and keeping only what is visible above the noise leaves a non-vanishing error (Corollary 1 ).

sections.heading: What this means in practice.
sections.text: The results suggest four rules for designing a truncated sampler. • Set the truncation level by the target accuracy, not by the noise level. Retain directions until their signal-to-noise ratio at the evaluation level falls to order ε / K \varepsilon/\sqrt{K} (Theorem 2 (c)). The resulting number of directions, of order ( C sp / ( η 2 ​ ε ) ) 2 / ( 2 ​ β − 1 ) (C_{\mathrm{sp}}/(\eta^{2}\varepsilon))^{2/(2\beta-1)} , can be estimated before training from the eigenvalues of the patch covariance, up to constants that depend on β \beta . • Run the diffusion below the evaluation level. Once the number of retained directions is fixed, the diffusion noise level should be set near the variance of the last retained direction, so that all retained directions stay above it and mix at comparable rates (Theorem 4 ). • Spend effort on the choice of directions rather than on the rates. On a fixed retained subspace, direction-dependent rates improve the sampling bound only by constants over equal rates (Proposition 3 ); what reduces the cost from the ambient dimension to the number of retained directions is which directions are kept. • Diagnose which error dominates. The error splits into a sampling part and a truncation part ( 10 ). A better score network reduces only the first; if the second dominates, the remedy is to retain more directions or to model the discarded ones.

sections.heading: Scope and limitations.
sections.text: The Gaussian replacement model isolates the cost of spectral truncation and admits matching bounds. For general data and mixtures, Section 5 provides upper bounds with explicit residual modeling terms. The end-to-end theorem uses exact scores to separate sampling and truncation from score learning; Theorem 3 quantifies the additional error for learned scores. The condition β > 1 \beta>1 ensures a dimension-independent moment bound, while the truncation analysis extends to β > 1 / 2 \beta>1/2 . Image spectra near β = 1 \beta=1 therefore call for retaining the finite spectral sums described in Appendix B.5 . The empirical PCA result establishes consistency under an oracle score and a small-perturbation condition. Patch-level guarantees extend to jointly modeled patches; independent generation incurs the cross-patch term in Appendix B.4 .

sections.heading: Further directions.
sections.text: The error decomposition suggests several extensions. For non-Gaussian data or learned residuals, useful lower bounds would account for both dependence and residual modeling accuracy; such results would complement the present Gaussian replacement benchmark. A coordinate-wise contraction analysis could also clarify when direction-dependent rates improve on equal rates, especially if weak directions are retained at small rates. Finally, wavelets ( Guth et al., 2022 ) and projection-pursuit directions ( Friedman and Tukey, 1974 ; Huber, 1985 ) offer alternative bases in which to study the same resolution-dependent trade-off.

sections.heading: A.1 Convergence theory for score-based diffusion models
sections.text: Score-based diffusion models estimate the scores of noised data marginals and use them in a reverse-time stochastic differential equation ( Anderson, 1982 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2020 ) . Polynomial convergence guarantees were obtained by Lee et al. (2022) ; Chen et al. (2022) ; Chen et al. (2023a) , and Benton et al. (2023) proved bounds that are nearly linear in the ambient dimension under finite second moments only. These results measure the cost of sampling in the dimension of the space in which the diffusion runs. Our convergence analysis (Theorem 3 ) extends the Girsanov argument of Chen et al. (2022) to diagonal anisotropic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, keeping the rate matrix throughout, so that the dimension enters through tr ⁡ ( Λ ) \tr(\Lambda) and the weighted second moment (Theorem 6 ).

sections.heading: Relation to truncation baselines.
sections.text: In the regime where our rates are used, all retained rates lie within a constant factor of λ 0 \lambda_{0} , so tr ⁡ ( Λ ) = Θ ⁡ ( K ) \tr(\Lambda)=\Theta(K) . The step count of Theorem 3 therefore coincides, up to constants, with what an existing dimension-linear bound gives when applied to the K K -dimensional coefficient law, for instance Benton et al. (2023) or Theorem 5 with r = K r=K ; Proposition 3 states this formally for equal rates on the same retained subspace. Our contribution is therefore not a faster sampler for a fixed K K . It is the analysis of the truncation itself: the cost of discarding directions (Theorem 1 ), the number of directions that must be retained (Theorem 2 ), and the resulting end-to-end prescription (Theorem 4 ). Whether direction-dependent rates can strictly improve on equal rates, for example by retaining weak directions with small rates, is left open (Section 7 ).

sections.heading: A.2 Low-dimensional and adaptive diffusion theory
sections.text: Several works show that diffusion models adapt to low-dimensional structure. Chen et al. (2023b) analyze score approximation and distribution recovery for data supported on a low-dimensional subspace, and Liang et al. (2025) obtain total-variation convergence governed by an intrinsic dimension. analyzes under the manifold hypothesis include De Bortoli (2022) ; Potaptchik et al. (2024) ; Azangulov et al. (2024) . A power-law covariance is different: it is generally full rank, so there is no intrinsic dimension to adapt to. Instead it defines a resolution-dependent count of relevant directions, which grows as the target resolution becomes finer. Our results quantify this count and show that it is larger than the number of directions visible above the noise level.

sections.heading: A.3 Spectral, subspace and multiscale diffusion
sections.text: Diffusion processes that treat spectral directions differently have been proposed and studied empirically. Subspace diffusion restricts later stages of the diffusion to lower-dimensional subspaces, such as principal or low-frequency components ( Jing et al., 2022 ) . Blurring and inverse-heat-dissipation models damp high frequencies faster than low ones ( Hoogeboom and Salimans, 2023 ; Rissanen et al., 2023 ) . Wavelet-based score models generate coefficients scale by scale ( Guth et al., 2022 ) . Matrix preconditioning has been used to accelerate score-based sampling ( Ma et al., 2022 ) ; there anisotropy serves speed, whereas here it enters the forward and reverse processes together and the question is which directions can be discarded. Our patch principal-component process with Wiener-gain rates belongs to this family. We do not propose a new architecture, and we do not claim that the Wiener-gain profile is an optimal schedule; our contribution is a theory that says how many directions such processes must retain and what discarding the rest costs.

sections.heading: A.4 Gaussian total-variation bounds and denoising
sections.text: Our lower bound relies on the two-sided total-variation bound for Gaussians of Devroye et al. (2018) , and the interpretation of the Wiener gain as the size of the data-dependent part of the score (Proposition 2 ) is an elementary consequence of Tweedie’s formula; the Wiener gain itself is the classical optimal linear shrinkage factor ( Torralba et al., 2024 ) . What we add is the combination of these tools into statements about truncated diffusion samplers. (i) For samplers that fill the discarded directions with noise, the eigenvalues that govern the Gaussian comparison are exactly the Wiener gains of the discarded directions, so the truncation error is a denoising quantity (Theorem 1 (a)). (ii) A projection argument turns the comparison into a lower bound for every sampler in this class: no accuracy on the retained directions compensates for discarded ones (Theorem 1 (b)). (iii) Under a power law this yields matching necessary and sufficient numbers of retained directions and an interpretable cut-off rule: the first discarded direction should have signal-to-noise ratio of order ε / K \varepsilon/\sqrt{K} , not of order one, so cutting at the noise level is provably insufficient (Theorem 2 , Corollary 1 ). (iv) Combined with the convergence analysis, the result gives an end-to-end prescription in which the resolution η \eta and accuracy ε \varepsilon determine K K , and K K in turn determines a diffusion noise level well below η \eta (Theorem 4 ). The sharp truncation results assume Gaussian data and apply regardless of the active sampler; exact scores are used for the end-to-end step count. The mixture extension gives an upper bound. Extending the matching lower bounds beyond Gaussian replacement is a direction for further work.

sections.heading: A.5 Natural-image statistics and patch models
sections.text: Natural images have approximately power-law spectra ( Field, 1987 ; Ruderman, 1994 ; Hyvärinen et al., 2009 ) , and patch Gaussian mixtures are a classical model of local image statistics ( Zoran and Weiss, 2012 ) . We use these facts to motivate the coefficient model of Section 2.1 ; they do not imply that a complete image is Gaussian or that its patch law factorises, and the corresponding residual and cross-patch errors remain explicit in our statements (Appendix B.4 ). The exponent that enters our bounds is the decay rate of the sorted patch-covariance eigenvalues, which differs from the Fourier exponent (Appendix B.5 ). Projection pursuit ( Friedman and Tukey, 1974 ; Huber, 1985 ) offers an alternative to principal components for choosing directions, which we leave for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix B Details of the Setup
sections.text: This appendix collects the material behind Section 2 : notation, the reverse-time dynamics and an explicit form of the sampler, the pixel-space and patch-level views, the exponent β \beta for images, the link between the smoothed target and early stopping, the proof of the error decomposition, and the relation between Wiener gains and scores.

sections.heading: B.5 The exponent β \beta for image patches
sections.text: The exponent in Assumption 1 is the decay exponent of the sorted covariance eigenvalues, not of the radial Fourier spectrum. For a stationary two-dimensional field with power spectrum S ⁡ ( f ) ∝ | f | − α S(f)\propto|f|^{-\alpha} , the number of frequencies with | f | ≤ F |f|\leq F grows like F 2 F^{2} , so the i i -th largest eigenvalue behaves like i − α / 2 i^{-\alpha/2} . The classical estimate α ≈ 2 \alpha\approx 2 for natural images ( Field, 1987 ; Ruderman, 1994 ) therefore suggests β ≈ 1 \beta\approx 1 for image patches, at the boundary of Assumption 1 , and β \beta should be estimated from patch covariances before the bounds are read quantitatively. The two halves of the analysis depend on β \beta differently. The truncation bounds of Section 3 use the power law only through tail sums ∑ i > K i − 2 ​ β \sum_{i>K}i^{-2\beta} , which are finite whenever β > 1 / 2 \beta>1/2 . The convergence bounds of Section 4 use β > 1 \beta>1 through ζ ⁡ ( β ) = ∑ i ≥ 1 i − β \zeta(\beta)=\sum_{i\geq 1}i^{-\beta} , which bounds the weighted second moment and the initial divergence; for β ≤ 1 \beta\leq 1 these quantities are instead bounded by the partial sum ∑ i ≤ K i − β \sum_{i\leq K}i^{-\beta} , which grows like log ⁡ K \log K for β = 1 \beta=1 and like K 1 − β K^{1-\beta} for β < 1 \beta<1 .

sections.heading: I.1 Empirical check of assumption 1
sections.text: Assumption 1 requires a two-sided power-law envelope c sp ​ i − β ≤ σ i 2 ≤ C sp ​ i − β c_{\mathrm{sp}}\,i^{-\beta}\leq\sigma_{i}^{2}\leq C_{\mathrm{sp}}\,i^{-\beta} with β > 1 \beta>1 ; it does not require the eigenvalues to follow one exact power law. This appendix checks the envelope, and the sign condition on β \beta , on the covariance spectra of natural-image patches. We ask three questions: (i) is the decay of power-law type rather than exponential (low-rank-like); (ii) how large is the envelope ratio C sp / c sp C_{\mathrm{sp}}/c_{\mathrm{sp}} , and does it hold on data not used to estimate β \beta ; and (iii) is the departure from a single power law, which the data clearly show, compatible with the way Assumption 1 is used in Sections 3-4. The short answers are: yes; C sp / c sp ≤ 2.42 C_{\mathrm{sp}}/c_{\mathrm{sp}}\leq 2.42 on the fitted range and ≤ 4.11 \leq 4.11 on the full spectral bulk, out of sample; and yes, because the departure is a broken power law, which satisfies the envelope by construction (Proposition 5 ), followed by a high-frequency roll-off that only affects the side of the envelope the analysis does not need there (Section I.1.4 ).

sections.heading: Patches.
sections.text: We use CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100( Krizhevsky et al. (2009) ), DIV2K ( Agustsson and Timofte (2017) ) and BSDS500 ( Martin et al. (2001) ). A patch is a random p × p p\times p RGB crop with values in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , vectorised to d = 3 ​ p 2 d=3p^{2} coordinates, for p ∈ { 8 , 16 } p\in\{8,16\} (CIFAR) and p ∈ { 8 , 16 , 32 } p\in\{8,16,32\} (DIV2K, BSDS500). Train, validation and test patches come from disjoint images (Table 1 ): CIFAR uses one patch per image; DIV2K and BSDS500 use 16 16 patches from each of 100 100 images per split ( 80 80 for the DIV2K validation split). BSDS500 uses its official split; for DIV2K the original training images are split 90 / 10 90/10 into train/validation and the original validation images form the test set.

sections.heading: Spectra and fitting window.
sections.text: On each split we compute the exact eigenvalues σ ^ 1 2 ≥ ⋯ ≥ σ ^ d 2 \hat{\sigma}_{1}^{2}\geq\dots\geq\hat{\sigma}_{d}^{2} of the sample covariance (global mean removed). Exponents are fitted by least squares on log ⁡ σ ^ i 2 \log\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{2} at 60 60 log-spaced ranks in a window [ ℓ , h ] [\ell,h] with ℓ = 8 \ell=8 and h = min ⁡ { d / 4 , ( n min − 1 ) / 4 , r num / 2 } h=\min\{d/4,\;(n_{\min}-1)/4,\;r_{\mathrm{num}}/2\} , where n min n_{\min} is the smallest split size and r num r_{\mathrm{num}} the numerically resolved rank. The cap at d / 4 d/4 and n / 4 n/4 keeps the window where sample eigenvalues estimate population eigenvalues reliably; ranks below 8 8 (mean luminance and colour directions) are examined separately.

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: On the common window we compare a power law log ⁡ σ i 2 = a − β ​ log ⁡ i \log\sigma_{i}^{2}=a-\beta\log i , an exponential law log ⁡ σ i 2 = a − λ ​ i \log\sigma_{i}^{2}=a-\lambda i , and the continuous broken power law of Definition 2 . The broken law’s breakpoint is chosen among 9 9 log-spaced candidates by validation error, and all three models are scored by mean squared error of log ⁡ σ ^ i 2 \log\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{2} on the test split.

sections.heading: The decay is of power-law type.
sections.text: Figure 2 shows the spectra on a log-log scale. Across the ten image cases, the exponential model has 2.4 2.4 - 20 20 times the test error of the power law (Table 2 ), so the spectra are not low-rank-like: every direction carries variance and the decay is polynomial, the regime Assumption 1 describes (see also Appendix A.2).

sections.heading: The exponent satisfies β > 1 \beta>1 .
sections.text: The fitted exponents lie in β ^ ∈ [ 1.24 , 1.85 ] \hat{\beta}\in[1.24,1.85] across all image cases and splits, and the three independent splits agree to within 0.11 0.11 (Table 2 ), so β > 1 \beta>1 , needed for the dimension-free moment bound of Section 4, holds throughout; the weaker condition β > 1 / 2 \beta>1/2 of the truncation analysis holds with a wide margin. β ^ \hat{\beta} decreases with patch size (Figure 4 a), from about 1.65 1.65 - 1.84 1.84 at 8 × 8 8\times 8 to 1.24 1.24 - 1.27 1.27 at 32 × 32 32\times 32 , approaching the value β ≈ 1 \beta\approx 1 suggested by the Fourier argument of Appendix B.5. Assumption 1 is stated for a fixed dimension d d , so we report its constants per patch size.

sections.heading: The envelope holds with small constants, out of sample.
sections.text: On the fitting window the envelope ratio is at most 2.42 2.42 for every image case and split (Table 3 ): over a range of up to 50 50 in rank, every eigenvalue lies within a factor of about two of a single power law. Figure 3 shows the compensated spectra; they are flat to within the two horizontal lines on the window and well beyond it, and the validation and test curves follow the training curve although β ^ \hat{\beta} was not fitted on them. Extending to the spectral bulk [ 8 , m ] [8,m] , which covers ranks up to m / d = 0.33 m/d=0.33 - 0.50 0.50 of the dimension for 8 × 8 8\times 8 and 16 × 16 16\times 16 patches, the ratio is at most 4.11 4.11 .

sections.heading: Low and high ranks.
sections.text: The two ends of the spectrum behave differently, and both are visible in Figure 3 . The first few eigenvalues (mean luminance and the colour-opponent directions) lie above the bulk envelope; including all resolved ranks raises the upper constant C C by at most a factor 6.9 6.9 (last column of Table 3 ), while the lower side holds there with margin ( σ ^ i 2 ​ i β ^ ≥ 0.60 ​ c \hat{\sigma}_{i}^{2}i^{\hat{\beta}}\geq 0.60\,c for i < 8 i<8 ). Beyond the bulk end m m , the spectrum rolls off faster than any power law with these exponents. This is the high-spatial-frequency end of the patch, where optical blur, anti-aliasing, demosaicing and JPEG quantisation remove energy; it lies below the envelope, so it violates only the lower side. sections.heading: I.1.3 The Broken Power Law and Why It Is Compatible with Assumption 1
sections.text: In every case the broken power law has the smallest validation error, and on the test split it improves on the single power law by a factor 1.1 1.1 - 6.8 6.8 in log-MSE (Table 2 ). The spectra therefore steepen gradually within the window; a single exponent is an idealisation. This does not conflict with Assumption 1 , which only asks for a two-sided envelope. Definition 2 (Continuous broken power law) . For A > 0 A>0 , a breakpoint b ≥ 1 b\geq 1 and exponents β 1 ≤ β 2 \beta_{1}\leq\beta_{2} , the continuous broken power law is σ i 2 = { A ​ i − β 1 , i ≤ b , A ​ b β 2 − β 1 ​ i − β 2 , i > b , \sigma_{i}^{2}\;=\;\begin{cases}A\,i^{-\beta_{1}},&i\leq b,\\[2.0pt] A\,b^{\beta_{2}-\beta_{1}}\,i^{-\beta_{2}},&i>b,\end{cases} or equivalently log ⁡ σ i 2 = log ⁡ A − β 1 ​ log ⁡ i − ( β 2 − β 1 ) ​ ( log ⁡ i − log ⁡ b ) + \log\sigma_{i}^{2}=\log A-\beta_{1}\log i-(\beta_{2}-\beta_{1})(\log i-\log b)_{+} . It decays like i − β 1 i^{-\beta_{1}} before the breakpoint and like i − β 2 i^{-\beta_{2}} after it, and is continuous at i = b i=b . The case β 1 = β 2 \beta_{1}=\beta_{2} is the exact power law (2). Proposition 5 (Envelope of a broken power law) . Proof. Let f ⁡ ( i ) = σ i 2 ​ i β f(i)=\sigma_{i}^{2}\,i^{\beta} . For i ≤ b i\leq b , f ⁡ ( i ) = A ​ i β − β 1 f(i)=A\,i^{\beta-\beta_{1}} is nondecreasing because β ≥ β 1 \beta\geq\beta_{1} ; for i ≥ b i\geq b , f ⁡ ( i ) = A ​ b β 2 − β 1 ​ i β − β 2 f(i)=A\,b^{\beta_{2}-\beta_{1}}i^{\beta-\beta_{2}} is nonincreasing because β ≤ β 2 \beta\leq\beta_{2} . sections.heading: What the data show.
sections.text: Every fitted broken law satisfies β ^ 1 ≤ β ^ ≤ β ^ 2 \hat{\beta}_{1}\leq\hat{\beta}\leq\hat{\beta}_{2} , so Proposition 5 applies with the single-law exponent. The ratio it predicts from the bend alone (column “broken law” in Table 3 ) accounts for 44 44 - 96 % 96\% of the observed log ⁡ ( C / c ) \log(C/c) ; the remainder is the small scatter of individual eigenvalues around the smooth law. The head exponents satisfy β ^ 1 ≥ 1.19 > 1 \hat{\beta}_{1}\geq 1.19>1 and the tail exponents β ^ 2 ∈ [ 1.87 , 2.54 ] \hat{\beta}_{2}\in[1.87,2.54] , so both pieces of the broken law individually satisfy the exponent condition of Assumption 1 . The breakpoint sits at a roughly constant fraction of the dimension, b ^ / d ∈ [ 0.05 , 0.17 ] \hat{b}/d\in[0.05,0.17] (Table 1 ), rather than at a fixed rank: the bend is the onset of the high-frequency roll-off described in Section I.1.2 , not a change of regime among low frequencies. The breakpoint is selected from a coarse grid of 9 9 candidates and should be read as a location, not a precise estimate.

sections.heading: I.1.4 Which Side of the Envelope the Analysis Uses
sections.text: The departures from an exact power law found above are of two kinds: a bounded multiplicative wiggle and bend in the bulk, and a roll-off below the envelope at the highest frequencies. The first is absorbed by the envelope constants (Proposition 5 , Table 3 ). For the second, note that the two sides of (1) enter the analysis in different places. • The upper side σ i 2 ≤ C sp ​ i − β \sigma_{i}^{2}\leq C_{\mathrm{sp}}i^{-\beta} is used for all ranks: it bounds the total variance by C sp ​ ζ ​ ( β ) C_{\mathrm{sp}}\zeta(\beta) (Section 4.1, Lemma 2) and the tail sums ∑ i > K x i 2 \sum_{i>K}x_{i}^{2} in the sufficiency part of Theorem 2, whose proof uses no other property of the spectrum. A spectrum that falls faster than i − β i^{-\beta} only decreases these quantities, so the high-frequency roll-off keeps every upper bound valid and makes the sufficient number of retained directions conservative. Empirically, the upper side holds on every resolved rank once C C is enlarged by the factor U ≤ 6.9 U\leq 6.9 of Table 3 . • The lower side σ i 2 ≥ c sp ​ i − β \sigma_{i}^{2}\geq c_{\mathrm{sp}}i^{-\beta} is used only for the retained directions i ≤ K ≤ d eff σ i\leq K\leq d^{\sigma}_{\mathrm{eff}} , where it keeps the rates of Theorem 3 bounded below, and on the block K < i ≤ 2 ​ K K<i\leq 2K , where it gives the necessity part of Theorem 2 and Corollary 1. Empirically, it holds with c / 2 c/2 on all ranks i ≤ m i\leq m , including i < 8 i<8 . Consequently the data support Assumption 1 in the form in which the analysis uses it: an upper envelope on all resolved ranks, and a lower envelope on the spectral bulk, which suffices whenever 2 ​ K ≤ m 2K\leq m . The sharp statements of Section 3 (Theorem 2, Corollary 1) and Theorem 4 are formulated for the exact power law (2); in the light of Table 2 , they should be read as describing the bulk exponent, with the constants of the envelope in place of C sp C_{\mathrm{sp}} . Theorem 1 needs no spectral model at all and can be evaluated directly on the empirical eigenvalues.

sections.heading: I.2 Empirical check of the truncation theory
sections.text: This appendix checks the results of Sections 3-4 on the model for which they are stated: centered Gaussian data with the exact power law (2). For this model every law involved is Gaussian, so total variation can be estimated directly from the densities, without a learned discriminator. We test, in order, the two-sided characterisation of the truncation error (Theorem 1), the number of retained directions and its exponents (Theorem 2), the cut-off rule (Theorem 2(c)), the failure of truncating at the noise level (Corollary 1), the absence of a dependence on d d , the lower bound for imperfect samplers (Theorem 1(b)) and the decomposition (10), and the exact-score sampler of Theorems 3-4. In short: every bound holds at every tested point; the truncation error equals 0.28 0.28 - 0.30 0.30 times the Wiener-gain tail norm; the fitted exponents agree with 2 / ( 2 ​ β − 1 ) 2/(2\beta-1) to within 1 % 1\% ; and the explicit sufficient choice K ε ​ ( η ) K_{\varepsilon}(\eta) is within a factor 1.5 1.5 of the true minimum.

sections.heading: I.3 Numerical study on image patches
sections.text: Theorems 1 and 2 are proved for Gaussian data with an exact power law, and Section 5 gives only upper bounds for mixtures. This appendix asks how well the Gaussian predictions describe a standard model of natural-image patches, for which every truncation error can be evaluated exactly. No sampler is trained: the retained coordinates are drawn from the data law itself, so all errors below are truncation errors TV ⁡ ( q ~ K η , q η ) \mathrm{TV}(\widetilde{q}^{\,\eta}_{K},q^{\eta}) of the ideal truncated sampler (Definition 1 with p = q K p=q_{K} ). Following Zoran and Weiss (2012), we model patches by a Gaussian mixture. All statements in this appendix are about the fitted mixture, not about the empirical distribution of image patches. All experiments were run on a single Apple M1 Pro MacBook, without a GPU.

sections.heading: Patches.
sections.text: For each of CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 we hold out 5,000 5{,}000 of the 50,000 50{,}000 training images for validation and fit on the remaining 45,000 45{,}000 ; the 10,000 10{,}000 test images are used only for evaluation. From each image we draw two 8 × 8 × 3 8\times 8\times 3 patches at random positions, giving 90,000 90{,}000 training, 10,000 10{,}000 validation and 20,000 20{,}000 test patches of dimension d = 192 d=192 . Pixel values are dequantised by adding uniform noise on each quantisation bin, and the mean training patch is subtracted.

sections.heading: Mixtures.
sections.text: We fit zero-mean Gaussian mixtures q = ∑ m = 1 M π m ​ 𝒩 ​ ( 0 , C m ) q=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\pi_{m}\mathcal{N}(0,C_{m}) with M ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } M\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\} components by EM. EM is initialised by 8 8 preliminary iterations and run for at most 100 100 iterations, or until the relative change of the training log-likelihood falls below 10 − 5 10^{-5} . A ridge of relative size 10 − 5 10^{-5} is added to every covariance, and components that collapse are reseeded. Table 8 reports the held-out log-likelihood gain over M = 1 M=1 in bits per dimension. With M = 32 M=32 the held-out log-likelihood exceeds that of a single Gaussian by 0.57 0.57 (CIFAR-10) and 0.64 0.64 (CIFAR-100) bits per dimension. Validation and test gains agree to within 0.01 0.01 bits per dimension for every M M , so the larger mixtures do not overfit. The gain is still increasing at M = 32 M=32 , but with diminishing returns ( + 0.02 +0.02 and + 0.03 +0.03 bits per dimension from M = 16 M=16 to 32 32 ). For M ≥ 8 M\geq 8 on CIFAR-10 and M ≥ 16 M\geq 16 on CIFAR-100, EM reached the iteration cap before meeting the tolerance. We use the M = 32 M=32 mixture as the data law throughout. Slower convergence affects how well the mixture approximates the data, not the validity of the comparisons below, which all treat the fitted mixture as the data law. sections.heading: I.3.4 How many directions
sections.text: Despite the excess error, the number of directions predicted from the covariance is accurate. Because the error decays steeply in K K , the excess error of the mixture translates into at most 19 % 19\% more directions. At ε = 0.01 \varepsilon=0.01 , the mixture needs between 4.8 4.8 and 18 18 times more directions than the k η k_{\eta} that lie above the evaluation level. Retaining only those k η k_{\eta} directions leaves an error between 0.16 0.16 and 0.56 0.56 , which increases with k η k_{\eta} as Corollary 1 predicts. Formally, the hypotheses of Corollary 1 and of Theorem 2(b) are not met here: the spectrum is not an exact power law, Corollary 1 requires k η ≥ 4 β + 1 ≈ 50 k_{\eta}\geq 4^{\beta+1}\approx 50 , and Theorem 2(b) requires ε < 1 / 200 \varepsilon<1/200 . The observations are therefore consistent with these results rather than a test of them. At coarse resolution the dependence on accuracy matches Theorem 2. Matching Bounds Under Power-Law Spectra Radmehr Karimian Ali Mohades Johannes Lederer Université de Genève Universität Hamburg Universität Hamburg Abstract Diffusion samplers can reduce computation by generating selected spectral coordinates and filling the remaining directions with noise. How many directions must they retain? We study this question for data with power-law covariance spectra. For Gaussian data compared to a smoothed target, we prove matching bounds on the required number of retained directions, provided that the ambient dimension is sufficiently large. The truncation error depends on the combined Wiener gains of the omitted directions, regardless of the accuracy of the sampler on the retained coordinates. Keeping only directions whose signal exceeds the output noise level can therefore leave a non-vanishing error: many individually weak directions remain significant in aggregate. Combining this characterization with a diffusion convergence bound yields sufficient sampling-step complexity under exact scores. The upper bounds also extend to estimated principal components and, componentwise, to Gaussian mixtures. The practical prescription is to select the retained subspace using an aggregate spectral-tail error budget, then to choose the diffusion noise level accordingly. 1 Introduction Diffusion models generate data by learning to reverse a process that gradually adds noise ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2020 ) . Their computational cost typically grows with the dimension of the space in which the diffusion runs, motivating approaches that exploit alternative representations of the data. Examples include diffusion in wavelet coordinates ( Guth et al., 2022 ) , frequency-dependent processes such as blurring diffusion and inverse-heat-dissipation models ( Hoogeboom and Salimans, 2023 ; Rissanen et al., 2023 ) , and diffusion restricted to lower-dimensional subspaces ( Jing et al., 2022 ) . Related approaches operate in learned autoencoder representations, including VAE-based latent spaces ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , which need not correspond to orthogonal transformations. Here, we focus on orthogonal representations, such as principal-component, Fourier, and wavelet bases, in which the distribution of signal across directions can be described explicitly. An orthogonal change of basis preserves the ambient dimension, but it can reveal a structure that a sampler can exploit. For images, a central example is spectral decay: natural-image spectra are often approximately described by power laws ( Field, 1987 ; Ruderman, 1994 ; Hyvärinen et al., 2009 ) . In a corresponding coefficient model, the variances satisfy σ i 2 ≍ i − β \sigma_{i}^{2}\asymp i^{-\beta} , so a small number of directions carry much of the variance, while many others contain progressively weaker signals. This unequal distribution of signals suggests that the effort needed to generate different coordinates should depend on their statistical importance. These observations motivate the question studied in this paper: how does spectral structure affect the convergence of diffusion samplers in an orthogonal representation and when can it reduce the sampling complexity? More specifically, under power-law spectral decay, how many directions must a sampler retain to achieve a prescribed accuracy at a given resolution, and how many sampling steps are sufficient on those directions? Answering these questions requires controlling both the convergence of the sampler on the retained coordinates and the approximation error from replacing the remaining coordinates with noise. Our analysis connects these two costs, quantifying when sampling complexity can be governed by the number of required directions rather than by the ambient dimension. Contributions. • The exact cost of truncation. For Gaussian data, replacing the discarded directions by noise costs, in total variation, a quantity of the order of the Euclidean norm of their Wiener gains g i = σ i 2 / ( σ i 2 + η 2 ) g_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{2}/(\sigma_{i}^{2}+\eta^{2}) , with matching upper and lower bounds (Theorem 1 ). The lower bound holds for every sampler of this kind, however accurate it is on the retained directions. • How many directions must be kept. Under a power law, accuracy ε \varepsilon at resolution η \eta requires, and is achieved with K ≍ β ( C / ( η 2 ε ) ) 2 / ( 2 ​ β − 1 ) K\asymp_{\beta}\bigl(C/(\eta^{2}\varepsilon)\bigr)^{2/(2\beta-1)} retained directions (Theorem 2 ), strictly more than the number of directions above the noise level. • End-to-end sampling complexity. For the reverse diffusion on the retained coordinates, with direction-dependent rates, the number of steps depends on the number of retained directions and not on the ambient dimension (Theorem 3 ). Choosing the diffusion noise level from K K gives O ~ ( ε − 4 β / ( 2 β − 1 ) ) \widetilde{O}\bigl(\varepsilon^{-4\beta/(2\beta-1)}\bigr) reverse steps with an exact score. The upper bounds extend to the principal components estimated from the data and to patch-based Gaussian mixtures (Section 5 ). Related work. Our lower bound is based on the two-sided total-variation bound for Gaussians of Devroye et al. (2018) ; what we add is the identification of the relevant covariance ratios with the Wiener gains of the discarded directions, and a projection argument that makes the bound hold for every truncated sampler. The convergence analysis extends the Girsanov argument of Chen et al. (2022) to anisotropic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. In the retained subspace, isotropic diffusion attains the same step count up to constants (Proposition 3 ), so the gain comes from choosing which directions to keep, not from how they are diffused. Preconditioned samplers ( Ma et al., 2022 ) use anisotropy to speed up sampling rather than to decide what to discard. A longer discussion is in Appendix A . Organisation. Section 2 introduces the data model and the truncated sampler. Section 3 proves the sharp bounds on truncation, and Section 4 the convergence of the sampler and its end-to-end complexity. Section 5 treats empirical bases and Gaussian mixtures. Section 6 reports experiments, and Section 7 discusses implications. 2 Problem Setup and Truncated Sampler We first fix the data model, then the diffusion that generates the retained coordinates, and finally the class of truncated samplers and the target against which they are judged. 2.1 Data model The covariance spectrum describes how the signal is distributed in different directions. We use a power-law envelope to allow unequal variances without imposing a low-dimensional support; Gaussianity is an additional condition for the sharp truncation results. Let X ∈ ℝ d X\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be a centered random vector with law q q and covariance C = V ​ diag ​ ( σ 1 2 , … , σ d 2 ) ​ V ⊤ C=V\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{d}^{2})V^{\top} , where V = [ v 1 , … , v d ] V=[v_{1},\ldots,v_{d}] is orthogonal and σ 1 2 ≥ ⋯ ≥ σ d 2 ≥ 0 \sigma_{1}^{2}\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{d}^{2}\geq 0 . In our application X X is an image patch of dimension d = D p d=D_{p} and V V is its principal-component basis. A full image split into N P N_{P} non-overlapping patches is handled patch by patch; generating all patches jointly replaces K K by N P ​ K N_{P}K below, while generating them independently adds a cross-patch error that we do not analyze (Appendix B.4 ). Assumption 1 (Power-law spectrum) . There are constants 0 < c sp ≤ C sp 0<c_{\mathrm{sp}}\leq C_{\mathrm{sp}} and β > 1 \beta>1 such that c sp i − β ≤ σ i 2 ≤ C sp i − β , i = 1 , … , d . c_{\mathrm{sp}}\,i^{-\beta}\;\leq\;\sigma_{i}^{2}\;\leq\;C_{\mathrm{sp}}\,i^{-\beta},\qquad i=1,\ldots,d. (1) The two-sided envelope allows for departures from an exact power law by fixed multiplicative factors. Every direction may carry positive variance, so no rank cut-off is imposed. The condition β > 1 \beta>1 makes the total variance bounded independently of d d , which is the property used in the convergence bound. It is not needed for the Gaussian comparison itself: the truncation rates require only β > 1 / 2 \beta>1/2 (Appendix B.5 ). The sharp results of Section 3 further assume that the data are Gaussian with an exact power law, q = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , C ) , σ i 2 = C sp ​ i − β , q=\mathcal{N}(0,C),\qquad\sigma_{i}^{2}=C_{\mathrm{sp}}\,i^{-\beta}, (2) which is the case c sp = C sp c_{\mathrm{sp}}=C_{\mathrm{sp}} of Assumption 1 . Gaussian patches are also the components of the patch Gaussian-mixture models commonly used for natural images ( Zoran and Weiss, 2012 ) , which we treat in Section 5 . For natural images, the exponent should be estimated from patch covariances; two-dimensional Fourier spectra suggest values of β \beta close to one (Appendix B.5 ). 2.2 Diffusion on the retained coordinates Once the retained subspace is chosen, sampling becomes a problem in the K K coordinates. We specify the forward process and its reverse discretisation here so that the later convergence bound applies to an explicit sampler. Fix a number K ≤ d K\leq d of the retained directions, let V K = [ v 1 , … , v K ] V_{K}=[v_{1},\ldots,v_{K}] , and write U = V K ⊤ ​ X ∈ ℝ K U=V_{K}^{\top}X\in\mathbb{R}^{K} for the retained coefficients, with the law q K q_{K} .
